units.translation: i.e. the scepter with which he steers, the rudder.
the directing scepter (ἰθυντήριον [directing] in some copies)

Thus Brunck. ἤθυνεν [he directed] in the first hand of M, ἴθυν [direct] by a corrector. Here and elsewhere in Aeschylus it is uncertain whether he preferred εὐθύνειν [to direct] or, which is not improbable, ἰθύνειν [to direct], and likewise in compounds and derivatives. Below at v. 860 I restored ἐπηύθυνον [they directed], since in M έπε.θυνον was written, with the u erased before the θ.
directing this winged bird by his judgment without bridles.
And Cyrus's fourth son directed the army.
Immediately he assigns honors to the gods.
And immediately their form and minds were distorted.
And he, as soon as he heard, announces this word to all the captains.
And immediately with the stroke of the dashing oar they struck the sea.
And immediately ship struck ship with bronze-armed beak.
Immediately let there be a purple-strewn passage.

where sense and meter require, comparing similar passages (and εὔφρονας πομπούς [kindly escorts] from Pers. 647), L. Dindorf restored εὔφρονι πομπᾷ [with kindly escort] in Thes. vol. 3 p. 2503. No less suspect is what follows at v. 1040 ἵλαοι δὲ καὶ εὐθύφρονες γᾷ δεῦρ᾽ ἴτε [come here, gracious and right-minded, to the land], where Meineke restored εὔφρονες αἴᾳ [kindly to the land].
come here, gracious and right-minded, to the land
αἱρετώτερος [more preferable] or εὐπορώτερος [more resourceful] is fr. 395.

since the antistrophic verse 706 δαφνοφόροισιν βουθύτοισι τιμαῖς [with laurel-bearing, ox-sacrificing honors] does not correspond to it, Hermann corrected in the strophe to προμαθίς [forethought], and in the antistrophe adopted Schuetz's emendation δαφνηφόροις [laurel-bearing]: which seems right.
